statement: Let $R$ be a [complete local ring](c:complete-local-ring) with [maximal ideal](c:maximal-ideal) $\mathfrak m$, let $f \in R[x]$ be a [polynomial](c:polynomial), and let $a \in R$ satisfy $f(a) \in \mathfrak m$ and $f'(a) \notin \mathfrak m$. Then exactly one $b \in R$ has $f(b) = 0$ and $b - a \in \mathfrak m$.

hypotheses.text: The ring $R$ is a [complete local ring](c:complete-local-ring): it is local with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$, and it is complete and separated in the $\mathfrak m$-adic topology.
The element $a$ is a root modulo $\mathfrak m$: $f(a) \in \mathfrak m$.
The root is simple modulo $\mathfrak m$: $f'(a) \notin \mathfrak m$.

conclusion: Exactly one $b \in R$ has $f(b) = 0$ and $b \equiv a \pmod{\mathfrak m}$.

proofs.name: Newton iteration
proofs.slogan: Run [Newton's method](c:newton-s-method) from $a$; the error squares at each step, so the iterates converge to a root.
proofs.scope: Existence and uniqueness of the root. For the ring of [p-adic](c:p-adic-number) integers $\mathbb{Z}_p$ with $\mathfrak m = p\mathbb{Z}_p$ it gives the classical lemma.

roles.why: Locality makes $f'$ invertible near $a$, completeness gives the limit of the iterates, and separation makes $f(b) = 0$.
The condition $f(a) \in \mathfrak m$ starts the induction at $f(a_0) \in \mathfrak m^{2^0}$.
The unit $f'(a)$ makes the Newton quotient defined and forces the root to be unique.

steps.slogan: Expand the [polynomial](c:polynomial) $f$ to second order around any point.
steps.detail: Expansion of each power $(x + h)^k$ gives $f(x + h) = f(x) + f'(x)h + h^2 g(x, h)$ with $g \in R[x, h]$. In particular $f(x) - f(y)$ is a multiple of $x - y$.

steps.slogan: Show that $f'$ is a unit at every point congruent to $a$.
steps.detail: If $x \equiv a \pmod{\mathfrak m}$, step 1 applied to $f'$ gives $f'(x) \equiv f'(a) \not\equiv 0$. In a [local ring](c:local-ring) every element outside $\mathfrak m$ is a unit, so $f'(x)$ is invertible.

steps.slogan: Define the Newton iterates and prove $f(a_k) \in \mathfrak m^{2^k}$ by induction.
steps.detail: Set $a_0 = a$ and $a_{k+1} = a_k + h_k$ with $h_k = -f(a_k)/f'(a_k)$, which step 2 allows. Then $h_k \in \mathfrak m^{2^k}$, and step 1 gives $f(a_{k+1}) = h_k^2\, g(a_k, h_k) \in \mathfrak m^{2^{k+1}}$; also $a_{k+1} \equiv a \pmod{\mathfrak m}$.

steps.slogan: Take the limit $b$ of the [Cauchy sequence](c:cauchy-sequence) of iterates and show $f(b) = 0$.
steps.detail: Since $a_{k+1} - a_k \in \mathfrak m^{2^k}$, completeness gives a limit $b$ with $b - a \in \mathfrak m$. By step 1, $f(b) - f(a_k) \in (b - a_k)R \subseteq \mathfrak m^{2^k}$, so $f(b) \in \bigcap_n \mathfrak m^n = 0$ because $R$ is separated.

steps.slogan: Compare a second root near $a$ with $b$ to show uniqueness.
steps.detail: If $f(c) = 0$ and $c - a \in \mathfrak m$, step 1 with $h = c - b$ gives $0 = h\,(f'(b) + h\,g(b, h))$. The second factor is congruent to the unit $f'(b)$ modulo $\mathfrak m$, so it is a unit and $h = 0$; with step 4, $b$ is the only root.

concepts.c:complete-local-ring: Completeness and separation give the limit root of the iterates.
concepts.c:maximal-ideal: Powers of the maximal ideal measure how small each correction is.
concepts.c:polynomial: A polynomial has an exact second-order expansion with coefficients in $R$.
concepts.c:newton-s-method: The iterates are the Newton steps $a - f(a)/f'(a)$.
concepts.c:p-adic-number: The p-adic integers are the main example of such a ring.
concepts.c:local-ring: In a local ring, elements outside the maximal ideal are units.
concepts.c:cauchy-sequence: The Newton iterates form a Cauchy sequence in the adic topology.

source.note: Newton's iteration, as in D. Eisenbud, Commutative Algebra with a View Toward Algebraic Geometry, Theorem 7.3.

statement: Let $A_1, \dots, A_n$ be events of a [probability measure](c:probability-measure) $P$ with $P(A_i) \le p$. Suppose each $A_i$ is mutually [independent](c:independence) of the events that are not its neighbours in a [dependency graph](c:dependency-graph) of maximum degree $d$, and $e\,p\,(d + 1) \le 1$. Then $P\big(\bigcap_i \overline{A_i}\big) > 0$.

hypotheses.text: A [dependency graph](c:dependency-graph) of maximum degree at most $d$ exists: each $A_i$ is mutually [independent](c:independence) of the family of events not adjacent to it.

conclusion: With positive probability no event occurs: $P\big(\bigcap_i \overline{A_i}\big) > 0$.

proofs.name: Induction on conditional probabilities
proofs.slogan: Bound the [conditional probability](c:conditional-probability) of each event, given that any set of other events fails, and multiply the bounds by the chain rule.
proofs.scope: The case $d \ge 1$, as the general local lemma with every weight $x = 1/(d + 1)$. For $d = 0$ the events are mutually independent with $P(A_i) \le 1/e < 1$, so the probability is $\prod_i (1 - P(A_i)) > 0$.

roles.why: The bound $P(A_i) \le p$ controls the numerator of the conditional probability.
Independence from the non-neighbours removes their condition, and degree at most $d$ leaves at most $d$ factors in the denominator.

steps.slogan: Show that $p \le x(1 - x)^d$ for the weight $x = 1/(d + 1)$.
steps.detail: The inequality $(1 + 1/d)^d < e$ gives $(1 - x)^d = (d/(d + 1))^d > 1/e$. Hence $x(1 - x)^d > 1/(e(d + 1)) \ge p$.

steps.slogan: Split a conditioning set $S$ into the neighbours $S_1$ of $i$ and the rest $S_2$.
steps.detail: Write $B_T = \bigcap_{j \in T} \overline{A_j}$ and claim $P(A_i \mid B_S) \le x$ for every $S \not\ni i$, by induction on $|S|$. Then $P(A_i \mid B_S) = P(A_i \cap B_{S_1} \mid B_{S_2}) / P(B_{S_1} \mid B_{S_2})$.

steps.slogan: Bound the numerator by independence of $A_i$ from the events in $S_2$.
steps.detail: $P(A_i \cap B_{S_1} \mid B_{S_2}) \le P(A_i \mid B_{S_2}) = P(A_i) \le p$, because $A_i$ is mutually [independent](c:independence) of the events indexed by $S_2$.

steps.slogan: Bound the denominator from below by the chain rule and the induction hypothesis.
steps.detail: For $S_1 = \{j_1, \dots, j_r\}$ with $r \le d$, $P(B_{S_1} \mid B_{S_2}) = \prod_t \big(1 - P(A_{j_t} \mid B_{S_2 \cup \{j_1, \dots, j_{t-1}\}})\big)$. Each conditioning set is smaller than $S$, so the product is at least $(1 - x)^r \ge (1 - x)^d$.

steps.slogan: Divide the two bounds to finish the induction step.
steps.detail: Steps 3 and 4 give $P(A_i \mid B_S) \le p/(1 - x)^d \le x$ by step 1. The same chain rule gives $P(B_S) \ge (1 - x)^{|S|} > 0$, so every condition is defined.

steps.slogan: Multiply the conditional bounds over all $n$ events by the chain rule.
steps.detail: $P\big(\bigcap_{i=1}^n \overline{A_i}\big) = \prod_{i=1}^n \big(1 - P(A_i \mid B_{\{1, \dots, i-1\}})\big) \ge (1 - x)^n > 0$, because $x < 1$ when $d \ge 1$.

concepts.c:probability-measure: All events and conditional probabilities live in one probability space.
concepts.c:independence: Mutual independence from non-neighbours makes the numerator at most $p$.
concepts.c:dependency-graph: The graph names the at most $d$ events that $A_i$ may depend on.
concepts.c:conditional-probability: The induction bounds conditional probabilities given that other events fail.

source.note: The proof of the general local lemma with all weights $1/(d+1)$, as in N. Alon and J. H. Spencer, The Probabilistic Method, Lemma 5.1.1 and Corollary 5.1.2.

statement: Let $L(q, \dot q, t)$ be a $C^2$ [Lagrangian](c:lagrangian) on $\mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}^n \times \mathbb{R}$, and let maps $h_s\colon \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ with $h_0 = \mathrm{id}$ form a [continuous symmetry](c:continuous-symmetry) of $L$. Then $I = \sum_i \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot q_i}\,\frac{d}{ds}\big|_{s=0} h_s(q)_i$ is constant along every solution of the [Euler-Lagrange equation](c:euler-lagrange-equation).

hypotheses.text: The maps $h_s$ form a [continuous symmetry](c:continuous-symmetry): $h_0 = \mathrm{id}$, $(s, q) \mapsto h_s(q)$ is $C^2$, and $L(h_s(q), Dh_s(q)\dot q, t) = L(q, \dot q, t)$ for all $s, q, \dot q, t$.
The path $q(t)$ is a $C^2$ solution of the [Euler-Lagrange equation](c:euler-lagrange-equation) $\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot q} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial q}$.

conclusion: The function $t \mapsto I(q(t), \dot q(t), t)$ is constant, so $I$ is a [conservation law](c:conservation-law) of the motion.

proofs.name: Differentiate the symmetry along a solution
proofs.slogan: Differentiate the invariance in the symmetry parameter along a solution, then replace $\partial L/\partial q$ by the Euler-Lagrange equation.
proofs.scope: Symmetries of the coordinates of a Lagrangian on $\mathbb{R}^n$. The field-theory version follows the same computation, with a divergence in place of the time derivative.

roles.why: A $C^2$ Lagrangian lets the chain rule act on $L$ and its partial derivatives be differentiated in $t$.
Invariance makes the derivative of $L$ in $s$ vanish.
The Euler-Lagrange equation turns $\partial L/\partial q$ into a time derivative.

steps.slogan: Move the solution by the symmetry to get the family $\Phi(s, t) = h_s(q(t))$.
steps.detail: Then $\Phi(0, t) = q(t)$ and $\partial_t \Phi(s, t) = Dh_s(q(t))\dot q(t)$. The invariance gives $L(\Phi, \partial_t \Phi, t) = L(q, \dot q, t)$ for every $s$.

steps.slogan: Differentiate the invariance identity in $s$ at $s = 0$.
steps.detail: The right side does not depend on $s$, so the chain rule gives $0 = \sum_i \frac{\partial L}{\partial q_i}\xi_i + \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot q_i}\dot\xi_i$ with $\xi(t) = \partial_s \Phi(0, t)$. Here $\partial_s \partial_t \Phi = \partial_t \partial_s \Phi$ because $\Phi$ is $C^2$.

steps.slogan: Replace $\partial L/\partial q_i$ by $\frac{d}{dt}\partial L/\partial \dot q_i$ along the solution.
steps.detail: The [Euler-Lagrange equation](c:euler-lagrange-equation) turns step 2 into $0 = \sum_i \big(\frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot q_i}\big)\xi_i + \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot q_i}\dot\xi_i$. All terms are evaluated at $(q(t), \dot q(t), t)$.

steps.slogan: Recognize the sum as the time derivative of $I$ by the product rule.
steps.detail: The right side of step 3 is $\frac{d}{dt}\sum_i \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot q_i}\xi_i = \frac{d}{dt} I(q(t), \dot q(t), t)$. A function with zero derivative on an interval is constant, so $I$ is a [conservation law](c:conservation-law).

concepts.c:lagrangian: The Lagrangian is the function whose invariance the proof differentiates.
concepts.c:continuous-symmetry: A one-parameter family of symmetries supplies the derivative in $s$.
concepts.c:euler-lagrange-equation: The equation of motion converts a partial derivative into a time derivative.
concepts.c:conservation-law: The conclusion is that the Noether charge $I$ is conserved.

source.note: The computation in V. I. Arnold, Mathematical Methods of Classical Mechanics, section 20 (Noether's theorem).

statement: For every $f$ in the [Lp space](c:lp-space) $L^2(\mathbb{T})$ of the circle $\mathbb{T} = \mathbb{R}/T\mathbb{Z}$ with its normalized [Haar measure](c:haar-measure), the [Fourier coefficients](c:fourier-coefficients) $\hat f(n) = \int_{\mathbb{T}} f(t)e^{-2\pi i n t/T}\,dt$ satisfy $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} |\hat f(n)|^2 = \int_{\mathbb{T}} |f|^2$, and the series converges.

hypotheses.text: The period satisfies $T > 0$, and the circle carries the [Haar measure](c:haar-measure) of total mass 1.
The function $f$ lies in the [Lp space](c:lp-space) $L^2(\mathbb{T})$.

proofs.name: Fourier Hilbert basis
proofs.slogan: The exponentials form an [orthonormal basis](c:orthonormal-basis) of the [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $L^2(\mathbb{T})$, so the coefficient map is an isometry onto $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z})$.
proofs.scope: The whole identity for every $L^2$ function. The completeness of the exponentials is the deep step, and it comes from the Stone-Weierstrass theorem.

roles.why: The normalized measure makes each exponential a unit vector.
Membership in $L^2$ makes $f$ a vector of the Hilbert space with finite norm.

steps.slogan: Check that the exponentials $e_n(t) = e^{2\pi i n t/T}$ are orthonormal in $L^2(\mathbb{T})$.
steps.detail: $\langle e_m, e_n \rangle = \int_{\mathbb{T}} e^{2\pi i (n - m)t/T}\,dt$ over a circle of total mass 1. This is 1 for $m = n$ and 0 otherwise.

steps.slogan: Show that the [trigonometric polynomials](c:trigonometric-polynomial) are dense in $L^2(\mathbb{T})$.
steps.detail: The span of the $e_n$ is a subalgebra of $C(\mathbb{T})$ closed under conjugation that separates points, so the Stone-Weierstrass theorem makes it uniformly dense in $C(\mathbb{T})$. Continuous functions are dense in $L^2(\mathbb{T})$, and uniform convergence implies $L^2$ convergence for a probability measure.

steps.slogan: Combine orthonormality and density into an [orthonormal basis](c:orthonormal-basis).
steps.detail: An orthonormal family with dense span is a Hilbert basis, so $f = \sum_n \langle e_n, f \rangle e_n$ in $L^2$. The coordinate $\langle e_n, f \rangle$ is exactly $\hat f(n)$.

steps.slogan: Transfer the norm of $f$ to its coefficient sequence by the basis isometry.
steps.detail: The coordinate map of a Hilbert basis is a linear isometry onto $\ell^2(\mathbb{Z})$. So $\sum_n |\hat f(n)|^2$ converges to $\|f\|_{L^2}^2$.

steps.slogan: Write the squared $L^2$ norm as the integral of $|f|^2$.
steps.detail: $\|f\|^2 = \langle f, f \rangle = \int_{\mathbb{T}} |f(t)|^2\,dt$. With step 4 this gives $\sum_n |\hat f(n)|^2 = \int_{\mathbb{T}} |f|^2$.

concepts.c:lp-space: The identity lives in the Hilbert space $L^2$ of the circle.
concepts.c:haar-measure: The normalized measure makes the exponentials orthonormal.
concepts.c:fourier-coefficients: The coefficients are the coordinates of $f$ in the exponential basis.
concepts.c:orthonormal-basis: A Hilbert basis turns the norm into a sum of squared coordinates.
concepts.c:hilbert-space: Completeness of $L^2$ makes the coordinate map an isometry onto $\ell^2$.
concepts.c:trigonometric-polynomial: Density of trigonometric polynomials makes the exponentials a complete family.

statement: For every [Schwartz function](c:schwartz-function) $f\colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ and every $x \in \mathbb{R}$, $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} f(x + n) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \hat f(n)\,e^{2\pi i n x}$, where $\hat f(\xi) = \int_{\mathbb{R}} f(t)e^{-2\pi i t \xi}\,dt$ is the [Fourier transform](c:fourier-transform); both series converge absolutely.

hypotheses.text: The function $f$ is a [Schwartz function](c:schwartz-function): it is smooth, and $x^k f^{(m)}(x)$ is bounded for all $k, m \ge 0$.

conclusion: $\sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} f(x + n) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} \hat f(n)\,e^{2\pi i n x}$ for every real $x$.

formal.difference: The declaration states only the equality of the two sums; their absolute convergence is proved inside the argument.

proofs.name: Periodization and Fourier series
proofs.slogan: Periodize $f$, compute the [Fourier coefficients](c:fourier-coefficients) of the periodization, and sum its [Fourier series](c:fourier-series).
proofs.scope: The whole formula for every real $x$, for the lattice $\mathbb{Z} \subset \mathbb{R}$, whose dual lattice is again $\mathbb{Z}$.

roles.why: Rapid decay of $f$ and of $\hat f$ makes both sums converge absolutely.

steps.slogan: Bound $f$ and $\hat f$ by a constant times $(1 + |x|)^{-2}$.
steps.detail: A [Schwartz function](c:schwartz-function) decays faster than every power, and its [Fourier transform](c:fourier-transform) is again a Schwartz function. So $|f(x)|, |\hat f(x)| \le C(1 + |x|)^{-2}$.

steps.slogan: Form the periodization $F(x) = \sum_n f(x + n)$ and show that it is continuous.
steps.detail: On a compact set $K$, $\sup_K |f(x + n)| \le C_K(1 + |n|)^{-2}$, a summable bound, so the series converges uniformly on $K$. Hence $F$ is a continuous [periodic function](c:periodic-function) of period 1.

steps.slogan: Compute the Fourier coefficients of $F$ as the values $\hat f(m)$.
steps.detail: Uniform convergence on $[0, 1]$ lets the sum pass through the integral: $\hat F(m) = \sum_n \int_0^1 f(x + n)e^{-2\pi i m x}\,dx = \int_{\mathbb{R}} f(t)e^{-2\pi i m t}\,dt = \hat f(m)$, because $e^{2\pi i m n} = 1$.

steps.slogan: Show that the coefficients $\hat f(m)$ are absolutely summable.
steps.detail: Step 1 gives $|\hat f(m)| \le C(1 + |m|)^{-2}$, and $\sum_{m \in \mathbb{Z}} (1 + |m|)^{-2}$ is finite.

steps.slogan: Sum the Fourier series of the continuous function $F$ at the point $x$.
steps.detail: A continuous periodic function with absolutely summable Fourier coefficients equals the sum of its Fourier series at every point. With step 3 this gives $\sum_n f(x + n) = F(x) = \sum_m \hat f(m)e^{2\pi i m x}$.

concepts.c:schwartz-function: Schwartz decay of $f$ and $\hat f$ makes every series converge.
concepts.c:fourier-transform: The right side samples the Fourier transform at the integers.
concepts.c:fourier-coefficients: The coefficients of the periodization equal the values $\hat f(m)$.
concepts.c:fourier-series: The formula is the Fourier series of the periodization at $x$.
concepts.c:periodic-function: Summing translates turns $f$ into a function of period 1.
